title: Mexico Owns the Water. Who Can Use It?
author: Meizhu Lui and Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla
content:
_This introduction by[Meizhu Lui](https://mexicosolidarity.com/author/meizhui-
lui/) and interview with [Luis Eugenio Parés
Sevilla](https://mexicosolidarity.com/author/luis-eugenio-pares-sevilla/)
originally appeared in the [October 21, 2026 edition of the Mexico Solidarity
Bulletin](https://mexicosolidarityproject.substack.com/p/mexico-solidarity-
bulletin-102126), the weekly publication of the Mexico Solidarity Project._

_Subscribe[here](https://mexicosolidarityproject.com/subscribe-contact/) to

![Greenpeace activists along the Santiago
River](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/02-greenpeace-
santiago.jpg)Greenpeace activists on a fact-finding and protest tour along the
Santiago River

### “Water everywhere… and not a drop to drink”

In Samuel Coleridge’s 18th—century English poem, sailors are stuck in the
middle of a windless sea, surrounded by water—but not a drop is drinkable to
assuage their agonizing thirst.

In the 21st century, the main problem isn’t salt water. The earth has always
provided fresh water—but now its use is monopolized by big industries. This
isn’t new. Back in 1995, when I went to the Fourth World Conference on Women
in Beijing, I heard a woman from the global south bemoan, “We have Coca-Cola,
Pepsi-Cola, RC-Cola—every kind of cola, but there is no water to drink.”

Today, in Jalisco, Mexico, the 400-mile-long Santiago River contains over
1,000 toxic chemicals, including not only heavy metals like arsenic, lead and
mercury but also cyanide, industrial waste, benzenes, chloroform, pesticides
and untreated municipal sewage. The Santiago once provided life-giving water;
now it provides death, disease and environmental destruction.

And just last week, on October 11 in Guadalajara, Jalisco’s capital, residents
poured into the streets to protest the foul-smelling black sludge emerging
from their faucets. Urban areas have their own problems, such as decaying
leaky pipelines that bring contaminated water to people’s homes. Not a drop to
drink.

The water supply crisis is growing not just in the Global South but in the
heart of the empire, the US. More than 300 US communities are demanding that
their local governments ban AI data centers because they consume enormous
amounts of water.

A human can live only up to three to seven days without water, and as Luis
Eugenio Parés reminds us, water is a finite resource. How long can humanity
last when we can’t find a drop to drink?

_Meizhu Lui, for the editorial team_

## VOICES

![Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/pares-headshot-640.jpg)

    
    
    Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla is a specialist in agricultural and agroindustrial planning, organization and development.  
    He has more than five decades of experience promoting projects for ejidos, communities and cooperatives that connect the social economy, technological innovation and food sovereignty to strengthen small producers. He is the author of books and articles on rural development, social organization and transformation of the Mexican agri-food system.

**How did people obtain water before the Mexican Revolution of 1910?**

In 1910, Mexico was predominantly a rural country. Residents collected water
directly from springs, rivers, natural pools, hand-dug wells, cisterns and
rainwater reservoirs. In semi-arid zones, they built _jagüeyes_ (earthen
reservoirs) and small dams; in the Yucatán Peninsula, _cenotes_ and cisterns;
and in Indigenous regions, community-based catchment systems and canals. Water
rarely reached homes on its own; people had to fetch, transport and store
it—and, whenever possible, boil or filter it.

![People filling their water jugs from a barrel in Rascón, San Luis
Potosí](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/04-rascon-1890.jpg)People filling their water jugs
from a barrel. Rascón, San Luis Potosí, ca. 1890 / W.H.Jackson

The Revolution’s 1917 Constitution introduced a decisive principle: Article 27
recognized national waters as the nation’s property, which enabled the post-
revolutionary State to construct large-scale dams, irrigation districts,
potable water systems and aqueducts.

**After 1917, how did the right to water change?**

In 1946, the State created the Secretariat of Hydraulic Resources to
coordinate the harnessing of all waterways and to utilize hydraulic
engineering for the country’s development. The nation viewed water as a
strategic public good—necessary for producing food and improving public
health.

![Young women in regional costumes on a Secretariat of Hydraulic Resources
parade float, Mexico City, circa 1950](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/05-srh-parade.jpg)Young women dressed in various
regional costumes during a parade on Avenida Juárez in Mexico City, circa
1950, representing the Secretariat of Hydraulic Resources.

In 1989, at the dawn of the neoliberal era, the government established the
National Water Commission, marking the start of a different management model.
It focused on regulating users, collecting fees, decentralizing services and
registering water “concessions.”

In a crucial turning point, under the 1992 National Waters Law, the nation
retained ownership of the water but consolidated the system of private
exploitation through concessions. These authorize the extraction of a specific
volume for a designated use, location and timeframe. A regulated market for
water rights emerged.

A fundamental distinction is that, legally, no one could buy or sell the river
or aquifer itself—only an authorized volume or concession, which granted
access to a scarce resource. The right to water increased the value of a plot
of land, an industrial facility or a real estate project. Water shifted from
being an essential requirement for life, collectively developed, to being an
industrial input—an economic asset for private profit. The right to use water
turned into a tradable commodity, and those uses generating the greatest
economic value got priority.

In short, prior to 1992, the State was responsible for distributing water—a
public good. From 1992 onwards, it functioned primarily as an office
responsible for issuing and registering access permits for private entities.

**Did free trade agreements further limit the access to water?**

Yes—they indirectly altered land and water use patterns.

Two simultaneous trends emerged in agriculture. On one hand, importing grains
produced with water from other countries is tantamount to importing the water
contained within them, which can alleviate local water stress. On the other,
the expansion of export crops (fruits, vegetables, berries, avocados, tomatoes
and beer) concentrates water extraction in irrigated regions, which reduces
the supply available for human needs.

![Water access in Mexico](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/06-drinking-water.jpg)Approximately 10 percent of the
Mexican population does not have access to drinking water.

Industrial discharges clearly cause water pollution. The Mexican Institute of
Water Technology examined the stretch of water between Lake Chapala, the Santa
Rosa Dam and the Santiago River and identified massive levels of pollutants.
Usual methods for cleaning the water aren’t sufficient; it would be akin to
using a kitchen colander to clean up paint and solvents. Community people who
live close to mines, Coca-Cola bottling plants and so on consistently protest
the lack of potable water for people and the environment.

**What is Mayor Clara Brugada’s response to the water crisis in Mexico City?**

Clara Brugada has made water a top infrastructure priority and introduced
several complementary strategies. For 2026, it announced a 7-billion-peso
investment in 643 projects covering potable water, drainage and sanitation.

The strategy combines citizen reports via the “H2O Line” with rapid-response
crews and equipment designed to detect underground leaks. The government aims
to triple the number of repairs compared to last year and replace sections of
deteriorated piping. The logic is sound: recovering a liter of water already
extracted and treated is generally cheaper (and more environmentally sensible)
than seeking a new source.

![H2O Line call center in Mexico City](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/07-h2o-line.jpg)H2O line call center. Photo: X
@GobCDMX

The city has launched a “100 water acupuncture points” program, featuring
absorption wells and rehabilitation of storm drains and small dams to capture
excess rainwater. It promotes rainwater harvesting in homes and public
buildings—a “sponge city” approach.

Treatment plant upgrades and expansions have increased water reuse. Treated
water can be used for industry, irrigation of green spaces, cleaning and other
purposes not requiring potable water. Every liter reused frees up higher-
quality water for human consumption.

**What about President Sheinbaum and her proposals to “recover” water?**

In September 2026, the [National Water
Commission](https://www.cakex.org/community/directory/organizations/national-
water-commission-comisi%C3%B3n-nacional-del-agua-conagua) (CONAGUA) reported
that reorganizing water concessions had enabled them to recover approximately
5 billion cubic meters of water. According to official estimates, this figure
is equivalent to the annual water supply for 90 million people, based on a
consumption rate of 152 liters per person per day.

![Presentation of the Government of Mexico's water
plan](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/08-water-
plan.jpg)The Government of Mexico presented its water plan for the coming
years

What, then, does “recovering water” mean? Primarily, it means that certain
volumes—previously under concession, underutilized, returned, regularized, or
consolidated—have changed their legal status regarding availability and can be
lawfully reallocated.

The reforms of the new General Water Law of December 2025 aim to limit the
transfer of water rights between private parties correcting the 1992 priority
on concessions in 1992. It puts in writing the human right to access,
availability and sanitation for domestic consumption. It asserts that water is
both a human right and a national asset.

But undeniable and unresolved challenges persist: aquifer overexploitation,
pollution, limited inspection capacity, insufficient budgets, weak municipal
services and inequality between rural and urban areas.

Ultimately, we judge a rights-based policy at the pipeline’s end: whether the
water arrives, whether it’s of good quality and reliable and whether it avoids
forcing a poor family to pay more than the cistern owner. The reform’s
ultimate test will be: do individuals and communities receive sufficient,
safe, reliable and affordable water?

**Is it necessary to frame the problem in a new way?**

Water operates in a continuous cycle. Paying attention to the entire
journey—from source to user—requires restoring forests, wetlands and soils;
offering compensation to _ejidos_ who conserve critical areas; requiring
large-scale consumers to pay for damage to water systems; promoting rainwater
harvesting and use of graywater; supporting local water committees; and
halting water-intensive projects where water is scarce. Above all, personal
and domestic consumption, ecosystems and food security must be the priority.

![La Angostura Dam on the Grijalva River in
Chiapas](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/09-angostura-
dam.jpg)La Angostura Dam near the Grijalva River in Chiapas. / Francisco
Cubas, megaconstrucciones.net

In short, water is neither created in an office nor guaranteed by words on
paper. It’s captured in the mountains and the soil, conserved within the
watershed, distributed via infrastructure, protected through budgets and laws
and shared through social agreements. If a step fails, the tap runs dry or
delivers contaminated water.

**Are the changes you recommend possible within a capitalist system?**

The extractivist capitalist model treats natural resources like land and water
as inexhaustible commodities, measuring their value solely by their
profitability. Thus, a forest is worth more when chopped down and an aquifer
worth more if it feeds industry. While a few capture the profits, local
communities and society bear the heavy cost of pollution, depleted resources
and lost livelihoods.

Nature doesn’t produce at market pace, nor does it recover at the speed
demanded by capital accumulation. Land needs time to regain its fertility;
forests require decades to regenerate; and aquifers can take hundreds or even
thousands of years to replenish. When extraction outpaces these natural
rhythms, it’s not true development—because the consumption practices of today
can make life impossible tomorrow.

When water ceases to be a commodity for profit-making, the human right to
water will become an everyday reality: a tap providing clean water, a
community with a future and a natural world capable of continuing to sustain
life.
